segments.say: Lesson 10. Chunking & Vector Databases. Fixed, recursive, semantic and parent-child chunking, plus how H N S W makes vector search fast.

Chunking is how you cut documents into pieces before embedding them, and a vector database is where those pieces live so the closest ones can be found in milliseconds. Here is an analogy. Cutting a textbook into index cards: too big and each card covers many topics; too small and a card loses its context. The card box (vector D B) has a clever index so you can find similar cards fast.

Why does this matter? Bad chunking is the number 1 hidden cause of poor rag answers. Choosing and tuning a vector store is a standard design question. A few key words. Chunk size / overlap: How big each piece is / how much neighbours share. Recursive splitting: Split by headings, then paragraphs, then sentences. A N N: Approximate nearest neighbour: fast, slightly inexact search. H N S W: The most common A N N index (a layered graph).
Chunking strategies. One runbook page: two sections with different topics. How should we cut it?
Fixed-size: cut every N tokens. Simple and fast, but chunk 2 mixes "Step 3" with Billing, so the topics blur.
Overlap (for example 10–20%) repeats the edge content in the next chunk, so a step that falls on a boundary survives.
Recursive: split on headings, then paragraphs, then sentences, only as small as needed. Each chunk equals one coherent topic. A great default (Lang Chain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter).
Parent-child / small-to-big: search over small, precise child chunks, but hand the L L M the whole parent section for full context.
Semantic: embed sentences and cut where meaning shifts (similarity drops). Better topic boundaries, but costs more at index time.

How H N S W search works. Brute-force search compares the query to every vector: O of n. Too slow for millions of chunks, so vector D Bs use A N N (approximate nearest neighbour) indexes like H N S W.
H N S W equals Hierarchical Navigable Small World graph: layers of linked vectors, sparse at the top and complete at the bottom.
Start at the top layer and take big "highway" jumps toward the query (like taking a flight between cities).
Drop down a layer and keep moving greedily to closer neighbours (now driving between towns).
At layer 0, walk local streets to the nearest match: E. That takes about log(n) hops instead of n comparisons.
Trade-off: A N N is approximate. Parameters like ef search and M trade recall against speed and memory.

Chunk size trade-off. Too small: precise matches but missing context ("Step 3" without knowing what it's for). Too large: more context but diluted embeddings, more tokens and more noise. Typical start: 300–800 tokens, 10–20% overlap, structure-aware. Then tune with retrieval evals, not vibes. Add metadata and contextual headers to each chunk (doc title, section path) so it carries context.

Vector database options. pgvector (Postgres): one D B for app data and vectors. Great if you already run Postgres or Supabase. Pinecone: fully managed and serverless. Weaviate / Qdrant / Milvus: open source, rich filtering, hybrid search. F A I S S / Chroma: libraries and lightweight stores for prototypes. Elasticsearch / OpenSearch: strong B M 25 plus vectors, good for hybrid search.

Index types. Flat: exact, brute force. Fine under ~100k vectors. H N S W: graph-based, high recall, fast, memory-heavy. The most common. I V F: cluster vectors and search only the nearest clusters. Less memory, tune nprobe. P Q (product quantization): compresses vectors to save memory, with some loss of accuracy.

Gotchas. P D F tables and code blocks get shredded by naive splitters, so handle them specially. Post-filtering after A N N can return fewer than k results. Prefer D Bs with pre-filtering or filtered H N S W. Forgetting to delete old vectors when a doc is updated.

Say it in the interview. "I start with structure-aware recursive chunking around 500 tokens with overlap, add the section path as metadata, and use parent-child retrieval when answers need surrounding context. For storage I'd pick pgvector if we're already on Postgres, or a managed store like Pinecone at large scale, with an H N S W index tuned for recall and metadata pre-filtering for permissions.".

Chunking strategies. Fixed-size: every N tokens, simple, predictable, splits mid-idea. Recursive: headings leads to paragraphs leads to sentences, coherent chunks, good default, depends on doc structure. Semantic: cut where embedding similarity drops, topic-pure chunks, slower, costlier indexing. Parent-child: search small, return big, precise plus full context, more storage and complexity. Document-specific: per-format (Markdown, code, tables), respects structure, custom code per type.
A N N indexes. Flat: slow at scale, low, 100% (exact). H N S W: very fast, high, very high. I V F: fast, medium, tunable (nprobe). I V F-P Q: fast, very low, lower.

A likely interview question: How do you choose chunk size? A strong answer: Start around 300–800 tokens with 10–20% overlap, structure-aware. Then tune using retrieval evals (recall@k, context precision) on a golden question set. Consider parent-child retrieval if answers need surrounding context.
That's it for Chunking & Vector Databases. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
